extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/political theory (those studying Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and interpretation of Plato's Republic (Books IV–V), extracting the political and ethical principles Plato (through Socrates) advances about the constitution of the ideal State, the parts of the soul, and related institutions (education, family, religion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the guardians take care of education, and education will take care of all other things; without education they may patch and mend as they please and will make no progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is the foundational institution of the State: it must form right habits and opinions so that citizens (especially guardians) do their duty. If education is defective, legislation and other remedies are ineffective; education fixes the 'ground' upon which laws apply (analogy of dye fixed on properly prepared cloth). Emphasis on long-term formation rather than short cosmetic measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of minute legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Minute enactments are superfluous in good states, and are useless in bad ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good political order depends on well-formed character and general principles, not on an endless catalogue of petty laws; excessive detail either unnecessary where virtue exists or ineffective where vice prevails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion rooted in highest conception and ancestral deity
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion shall be based on the highest conception of the gods and the true national or Hellenic type; no foreign god shall be supreme in our realms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious policy should promote the best conception of the divine compatible with national character; religion is treated briefly but is expected to support civic order and virtue rather than sectarian variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty before happiness (ethical priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: First duty, then happiness, is the natural order of our moral ideas; the State's primary aim was not to make citizens happy but to make them guardians doing their duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political/ethical design privileges obligation and right over individual pleasure or utilitarian happiness. Utility has corrective value but is secondary to right and truth; virtue may even require self-sacrifice where subjective happiness diverges from duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right/truth above mere utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The utilitarian principle is valuable as a corrective, but 'the greatest happiness' is not the true foundation of ethics; right and truth are the highest aims of government as well as individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and moral judgement should appeal to ideals of right and truth and not reduce everything to expediency. Where possible the most honourable (and sacred) should be the most beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, harmony, proportion as foundational principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of a whole lies at the foundation of politics and of art, supplying the principle of criticism under names of harmony, symmetry, measure, proportion, unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both political order and aesthetic judgment require recognition of unity and proportion: classes and parts must be in proper relation to the whole. This principle underlies criticisms of size, division of labour, and civic arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit state size (Greek model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The State should be limited in size, after the traditional model of a Greek state (the cities of Hellas were small and that fact is converted into a principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small scale is presented as a precondition of the proper functioning of the political whole (cohesion, harmony, manageability); large polities risk dilution of these virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour and 'every one doing his own' (definition of justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is 'every one having his own'—the great object of government is that every man should do his own business; injustice is every man doing another's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and individual justice is functional: stability and justice arise from people occupying appropriate roles. While some mobility or overlap is not fatal, the state's wellbeing depends on the right man in the right place; the example warns against craftsmen becoming guardians and against concentration of incompatible functions in one person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four cardinal virtues as criteria for State and soul
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect State contains wisdom, courage, temperance, justice; each corresponds to classes in the State and parts of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These virtues serve as diagnostic standards: wisdom concentrated in guardians (policy skill), courage in soldiers (fixed right opinion about danger), temperance as harmony/self-mastery across classes, and justice as the universal order allowing each part to do its work. The State and the individual are judged by presence and proper relation of these virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom concentrated in a small ruling class (guardians)
rubrics_metrics.description: The guardians are a small class far smaller than craftsmen; in them is concentrated the wisdom of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulership requires specialized policy skill that differs from manual or technical crafts. The guardians' education and selection should secure that wisdom; the small number amplifies concentrated knowledge and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage as stabilized right-opinion about danger (political courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is the never-failing salvation of the opinions which law and education have prescribed concerning dangers—fixed by proper education and laws (the 'ground' laid by education and the 'dye' by laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage is not mere animal bravery but a civil/political quality rooted in durable beliefs about what is dangerous or honourable; laws and education must instil and fix those beliefs so they resist pleasure, pain or fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as harmony/mastery of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance suggests harmony: the better principle mastering the worse; temperance is the harmony diffused through the whole making dwellers one in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is evaluated as concord between rulers and subjects and internal order in individuals; it is less a separate power than a harmonious relation that keeps spirited and appetitive elements in check via reason's leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice defined as harmony of functions (the right man in the right place)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the perfect order by which all natures and classes do their own business—the right man in the right place, the division and co-operation of all citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is assessed by systemic order: absence of theft, falsehood, adultery, impiety, i.e., when each part performs its role. It is the culmination of harmony among virtues rather than an additional isolated trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite soul: rational, irascible (spirit), concupiscent (desire)
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul has three parts—reason, spirit (irascible), and desire—which correspond to the three classes of the State; their distinct impulses and interactions justify treating them separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological diagnosis is a basis for moral education and political design: recognizing separate faculties explains contradictory impulses and motivates different educational treatments (reason rules, spirit supports reason against passion, desire must be restrained). The empirical examples (thirst vs reason, Leontius) illustrate the separability of motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education combining music and gymnastics to harmonize the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason, the superior, and passion, the inferior, will be harmonized by the influence of music and gymnastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balanced curriculum—musical education for the soul's refinement and gymnastics for bodily discipline—is the prescribed method to align the soul's parts and produce temperate, courageous, wise citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of education and shared duties for women (where aptitudes equal)
rubrics_metrics.description: If women are to have the same employments as men, they must have the same education—music, gymnastics, and the art of war; women are the same in kind as men and possess the same aptitudes, though often in less degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gender-differentiated presuppositions do not justify excluding women from public roles; selection should be talent-based. Expect social discomfort or ridicule but insist on habit and training overturning prejudices. Women chosen for guardianship should be trained equivalently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal households and community of wives/children among guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: After selection, guardians will dwell in common houses, have common meals, and wives and children will be shared—private families are abolished among guardians to secure unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communalization promotes unity by removing private interests that produce discord. The practicalities include regulated festivals for mating, controlled pairings, and measures to prevent mothers recognizing their own children; these arrangements are defended as conducive to the greatest good of State unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-directed eugenic selection and regulated reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers will contrive pairings (by lots and devices) so the brave and fair come together and the inferior are paired with inferiors; offspring of the good are reared, others destroyed; rulers may employ controlled falsehoods to conceal their intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproduction is treated as a matter of public policy to preserve civic excellence. The scheme includes timed hymeneal festivals, selection of parents in prime age ranges, and opaque mechanisms to hide the rulers' manipulations—ethical controversy acknowledged but justified by perceived civic benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and legal regulation of mating (population control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents ought to be in the prime of life (men ~25–55, women ~20–40); anyone outside these ages participating in hymeneals is guilty of impiety; marriages outside approved times require rulers' consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproductive participation is legally regulated to optimize child-bearing and population quality; legal sanctions enforce timing and consents to align individual behaviour with state demographic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity as supreme civic good; elimination of private interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest good of a State is unity; the greatest evil is discord and distraction. Unity is achieved where there are no private pleasures/pains/interests so that every citizen is tied to every other by common bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies (common meals, common housing, naming conventions, shared parenthood) aim to make citizens feel kinship and mutual sensitivity so injurious local or private interests do not fracture the whole. Language and ritual reinforce the reality of communal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers may use noble falsehoods for social engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulers must be skilful physicians of the State, for they will often need a strong dose of falsehood to bring about desirable unions between their subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deception (a 'noble lie' or engineered myths) is presented as an instrument for social cohesion and to conceal the mechanics of selection; its use is framed as a pragmatic tool of statesmanship rather than mere mendacity.
